title: Cascade Customer Support — reference call playbook sync
summary: CS-led prep for using Cascade as a reference customer. Aligned on (1) what Cascade is comfortable sharing on reference calls, (2) scheduling constraints and a cooldown policy, and (3) topics to avoid given prior escalations (availability incident + a billing confusion). Redwood will provide a tighter call brief, handle all scheduling through CS, and avoid pulling Cascade into “security deep dive” calls. Cascade is open to 1–2 reference calls/month for late-stage deals, focused on support-agent productivity use cases (chat + embeddings) and Redwood’s operational tooling (Console dashboards, fallbacks).
topics: Reference program scope (calls only vs public case study)
Call boundaries: approved topics vs avoid list
How Redwood will brief prospects and log outcomes
Handling security/SLA questions without putting Cascade on the spot

Cascade (Jules) to confirm who can be on calls (primary + backup) and preferred timeslots by 2025-10-27.
Redwood (Tyler) to add Cascade reference limits + cooldown notes to tracking sheet/HubSpot fields by 2025-10-25.

transcript:
Fireflies.ai — Transcript

Title: Cascade Customer Support — reference call playbook sync
Date: 2025-10-22
Time: 3:02pm PT
Duration: 38 minutes

Attendees
Redwood Inference: Miguel Santos (Customer Success), Rachel Kim (CS Readiness & Approvals), Tyler Benson (Marketing Ops)
Cascade Customer Support: Jules Harding (Director, Support Ops), Mina Cho (Eng Manager, AI Platform)

---

[00:00] Miguel Santos: Cool. Alright, I think we’re recording. Thanks both for making time. This is, um, pretty tactical. We’ve got a reference program ramping and we want to do it in a way that’s not annoying for you, and also doesn’t pull you into any topics you don’t wanna be on the hook for.

[00:16] Jules Harding: Yep. Love that framing.

[00:18] Mina Cho: Yeah, and just to level set, I can stay for like 30-ish. I’ve got a deploy window at four.

[00:23] Miguel Santos: Perfect. We’ll keep it tight.

[00:26] Rachel Kim: Hey everyone. Rachel here. I’m mostly listening, but I’ll jump in on guardrails and the “avoid list.”

[00:32] Tyler Benson: And Tyler — I’m the person who annoys you with forms, but I’ll try not to.

[00:36] Jules Harding: (laughs) We can handle one form.

[00:40] Miguel Santos: Great. So, goal today: confirm (1) are you open to reference calls, (2) how many per month is realistic, (3) what topics are green/yellow/red, and (4) logistics — scheduling, lead time, who from Cascade should join.

[00:57] Jules Harding: Okay.

[01:00] Miguel Santos: Quick context on what we mean by reference call: Redwood has a late-stage prospect, the AE asks us for a customer they can talk to. We pre-brief both sides. Usually it’s 20 to 30 minutes, on Zoom, and the prospect asks “what’s it like in prod?” That’s it.

[01:16] Jules Harding: Yeah, that’s fine. I just don’t want it to become an interrogation or like, security review-by-proxy.

[01:22] Rachel Kim: Exactly. That’s one thing we can prevent by gating which deals can request you.

[01:28] Miguel Santos: Right. We’ll talk about that.

[01:30] Miguel Santos: Before anything — are you open to doing calls only, or also a public case study with logo and quotes?

[01:38] Jules Harding: Calls only for now.

[01:40] Mina Cho: +1. We’re not in a place to publish metrics publicly. And honestly, we’ve got a couple internal things… I don’t want public scrutiny.

[01:48] Miguel Santos: Totally fair. Calls-only still helps a lot.

[01:52] Tyler Benson: And just to be explicit — calls-only is fine. We track those separately and we can do a “private reference” label.

[02:00] Miguel Santos: Cool. So on volume: what’s the max that doesn’t burn you out? Some customers say “one a quarter” and some say “two a month.”

[02:10] Jules Harding: Two a month is probably the ceiling. One a month is more comfortable.

[02:15] Mina Cho: I’d prefer not to be on every call. I can join the more technical ones but I can’t be the default.

[02:21] Miguel Santos: Makes sense. What if we set policy: up to 2 calls/month, but we aim for 1; and you have a “cooldown” — like no back-to-back weeks.

[02:30] Jules Harding: Yeah, and also, like, not on Fridays.

[02:33] Miguel Santos: (laughs) I support that.

[02:35] Rachel Kim: We’ve been implementing a cooldown across the program. Typically: at least 10 business days lead time, and not more than 1 call per week.

[02:45] Jules Harding: Ten business days might be a lot, but… maybe. Our calendar is a mess.

[02:50] Miguel Santos: We can do 7 business days as the target, and 10 as “best effort.” Like, we’ll avoid “we need it tomorrow.”

[02:58] Jules Harding: Okay. That helps.

[03:02] Tyler Benson: And to reduce scheduling churn, we can collect two “office hours” windows a month from you, and only offer those to prospects.

[03:09] Jules Harding: That would be ideal.

[03:11] Miguel Santos: Great. Jules, do you have preferred days/times?

[03:15] Jules Harding: Tuesdays and Wednesdays, 10 to noon Pacific, generally.

[03:21] Mina Cho: Wednesday 10:30 to 11:30 is safest for me.

[03:26] Miguel Santos: Perfect. We’ll lock those as primary.

[03:29] Miguel Santos: Okay, content. Let’s talk “green list” — what you’re comfortable discussing.

[03:35] Jules Harding: We can talk about the use case. Like, we built an agent assist thing. It drafts replies, does summarization, pulls articles. That’s fine.

[03:44] Mina Cho: Technically we can talk about the integration pattern too — we’re using your chat endpoint, embeddings, and rerank. And we’re doing some caching on our side.

[03:53] Miguel Santos: Great. Do you want to mention which models?

[03:57] Mina Cho: I’d rather not name the exact model SKU, because we’ve switched a couple times.

[04:02] Miguel Santos: Totally. We can keep it at “open model family” and “Redwood-managed model routing.”

[04:08] Rachel Kim: Also avoids the “but you said X model” gotchas.

[04:11] Jules Harding: Yeah.

[04:13] Miguel Santos: How about performance outcomes? Even qualitative, like “it got faster” or “more stable.”

[04:19] Jules Harding: Qualitative is okay. No numbers.

[04:22] Mina Cho: Yeah. We can say “we hit our latency target” but we can’t say “p95 is 300ms.”

[04:27] Miguel Santos: Got it.

[04:29] Tyler Benson: If a prospect asks for numbers, can we give ranges? Like “sub-second” or “hundreds of milliseconds”?

[04:36] Jules Harding: “Sub-second” is okay.

[04:38] Mina Cho: “Hundreds of milliseconds” is probably too specific. Just say “sub-second for typical requests,” something like that.

[04:45] Rachel Kim: Perfect. We have approved safe language. I’ll send it.

[04:49] Miguel Santos: Great. Now, “red list” — topics to avoid. I’m going to say a couple out loud and you tell me if I’m missing any.

[04:57] Miguel Santos: One is the incident we had in… I think late August? The latency spike / intermittent 5xx. We shouldn’t bring that up.

[05:06] Jules Harding: Please, yes, do not bring that up.

[05:08] Mina Cho: Yeah. And also the billing issue we had where the invoice looked weird — that was mostly a misunderstanding but it became a thread.

[05:15] Miguel Santos: Yep. We’ll avoid pricing and invoices.

[05:18] Rachel Kim: Also avoid anything that sounds like an SLA commitment from Cascade. Like “we get 99.9.” That’s Redwood’s job, not yours.

[05:25] Jules Harding: Thank you.

[05:27] Miguel Santos: Any product roadmap topics you want to keep off-limits? Like “are you building X feature,” “are you moving to Dedicated,” etc.

[05:34] Mina Cho: Yeah, no roadmap. No “we’re adding voice” or whatever. It changes.

[05:39] Jules Harding: And no internal metrics like ticket deflection or agent handle time. Those are sensitive.

[05:45] Miguel Santos: Got it. So: avoid incident history, avoid pricing/billing, avoid internal support KPIs, avoid roadmap.

[05:52] Tyler Benson: Also no security posture statements that you haven’t approved, like “we’re HIPAA” or “we’re SOC2” — unless you want to.

[06:00] Jules Harding: Yeah, don’t talk about our compliance.

[06:02] Miguel Santos: Cool.

[06:03] Miguel Santos: What about “why Redwood” — what’s the honest story that we can tee up?

[06:09] Jules Harding: Reliability and being able to see what’s happening. The console has been useful for us when our PM freaks out.

[06:16] Mina Cho: And honestly, the implementation was easier than I expected. The API was consistent. We didn’t have to stitch five vendors.

[06:24] Miguel Santos: That’s great. If a prospect asks “why not OpenAI or Anthropic direct,” what do you say?

[06:31] Mina Cho: We wanted more control. Like, on routing and fallbacks. And cost predictability.

[06:36] Jules Harding: And we didn’t want to keep rewriting prompts every time we switch models. Having one layer helps.

[06:42] Miguel Santos: Perfect. That maps to our messaging.

[06:46] Rachel Kim: I also want to protect you from being used as a “proxy SE.” So we’ll tell prospects: this is business/user experience, not a technical architecture review.

[06:56] Mina Cho: Please.

[06:58] Miguel Santos: Mina, are there any technical topics that are okay, like “we use streaming,” “we do tool calling,” etc.

[07:06] Mina Cho: Streaming is fine. Tool calling… we do some function calling but I don’t want to go deep. They can ask “do you support it,” yes. But don’t make me walk through our entire stack.

[07:17] Miguel Santos: Makes sense.

[07:19] Tyler Benson: We can add a “stoplight” section in the brief: green/yellow/red.

[07:23] Jules Harding: That would help.

[07:25] Miguel Santos: On who attends: Jules, would you be the primary, and Mina is optional?

[07:31] Jules Harding: Yes. I can handle most. If it’s a super technical buyer, we can pull Mina in if available.

[07:38] Mina Cho: Yep.

[07:40] Miguel Santos: Great. We’ll also have a Redwood person always on the call, just to moderate and timebox.

[07:47] Jules Harding: That’s important. I don’t want to be the bad guy ending the call.

[07:51] Miguel Santos: Yep. We’ll do intro, set expectations, and do time checks.

[07:56] Rachel Kim: And we’ll do a pre-brief with the prospect and the AE: “Do not ask about outages, do not ask about internal KPIs,” etc.

[08:04] Jules Harding: Thank you.

[08:06] Miguel Santos: Let’s talk about what a “good” prospect fit is. Like, which types of deals should be allowed to request Cascade.

[08:13] Jules Harding: Similar use case — support, customer service automation, agent assist.

[08:18] Mina Cho: Or anyone using chat + embeddings in production. But not someone wanting like, hardcore regulated security conversations.

[08:26] Rachel Kim: Great. We can create a rule: “Cascade is not a security reference.” We’ll route those to other customers or Redwood Security.

[08:33] Tyler Benson: We can also put a note in the intake form: if the AE selects “security deep dive needed,” Cascade won’t show up.

[08:40] Miguel Santos: Perfect.

[08:42] Miguel Santos: One more thing — logging. After a reference call, we log the date, deal name, and a short outcome. Is that okay? It’s internal only.

[08:51] Jules Harding: Yeah. Just no recording shared with prospects.

[08:55] Miguel Santos: Agreed. No sharing recordings. Redwood can record for internal note-taking but we won’t distribute.

[09:01] Mina Cho: Honestly, I’d prefer no recording at all.

[09:04] Rachel Kim: We can do notes-only for Cascade calls. That’s totally fine.

[09:08] Miguel Santos: Done. We won’t record these.

[09:11] Tyler Benson: I’ll mark that as a hard rule in the tracker.

[09:13] Jules Harding: Thank you.

[09:15] Miguel Santos: Okay. Let’s roleplay a little. Common prospect questions we see: “How long did it take to integrate?” “What broke?” “How’s support?” “Do you get surprise cost spikes?”

[09:27] Jules Harding: Support has been good. You guys respond. But I’m not going to say “always in 10 minutes.”

[09:34] Miguel Santos: Totally.

[09:36] Mina Cho: Integration was like… I don’t know, a couple weeks to MVP.

[09:40] Jules Harding: But don’t quote us.

[09:41] Mina Cho: Yeah, don’t quote me. (laughs)

[09:44] Miguel Santos: We can say “weeks, not months.”

[09:47] Jules Harding: That’s fine.

[09:49] Rachel Kim: And “what broke” — we should preemptively say we’re not going to discuss past incidents, but we can discuss how we manage reliability now.

[09:57] Jules Harding: That’s a good line.

[10:00] Miguel Santos: Exactly. Like “we have monitoring, alerting, and Redwood has fallback routing.”

[10:06] Mina Cho: Yeah, the fallback thing is real. When one model had weird output, you helped route us to a different variant. That was good.

[10:14] Miguel Santos: Great. That’s safe to say.

[10:16] Tyler Benson: Do you mind if we mention Redwood Console dashboards? Like token cost and latency breakdown.

[10:22] Jules Harding: That’s fine.

[10:24] Mina Cho: Yeah. Just don’t show screenshots from our account.

[10:27] Miguel Santos: Of course.

[10:29] Rachel Kim: For the “metrics question,” we’ll align on a standard answer: “we can share qualitative results; we’re not sharing exact numbers publicly.”

[10:38] Jules Harding: Perfect.

[10:40] Miguel Santos: Okay. Any other sensitive topics? Sometimes prospects ask “what do you pay” or “what commit.”

[10:47] Jules Harding: Hard no.

[10:49] Miguel Santos: Great.

[10:51] Miguel Santos: Let’s land the scheduling mechanics. Tyler can you explain what the intake looks like on our side?

[10:56] Tyler Benson: Yep. An AE fills a short form: deal stage, expected call date range, what they want to learn, and a “do not ask” acknowledgement. Then it routes to Miguel/Rachel to approve. Then Miguel reaches out to Jules with 2–3 proposed slots inside your office hours.

[11:14] Jules Harding: Okay, and that means I’m not getting random emails from five sales people.

[11:18] Tyler Benson: Correct. One thread, always through CS.

[11:21] Miguel Santos: And if you ever say “pause,” we pause. No questions.

[11:25] Jules Harding: Great.

[11:27] Mina Cho: Can we also do like, a short pre-brief doc? Like, tell us who the prospect is and what they’re building.

[11:33] Miguel Santos: Absolutely. We’ll send a one-pager: company, use case, why they asked for you, and the top 5 questions we expect.

[11:41] Rachel Kim: And we’ll include the stoplight section and the “if asked, say this” scripts.

[11:47] Jules Harding: Sounds good.

[11:49] Miguel Santos: Cool. I think that covers it. Mina, anything else before you drop?

[11:55] Mina Cho: Just reiterating — no recording, no screenshots, no model SKU, no internal metrics.

[12:02] Miguel Santos: Got it. Thank you.

[12:04] Mina Cho: Alright, I’m gonna bounce. Thanks.

[12:06] Miguel Santos: Thanks, Mina.

[12:07] (Mina left the meeting)

[12:10] Miguel Santos: Jules, last bit — incentives. We’re not doing anything weird, but we can offer stuff like conference credit or donation. Do you care?

[12:19] Jules Harding: It’s nice, but it’s not required. If there’s a donation option, that’s easiest internally.

[12:25] Tyler Benson: Great. We have a donation option. I’ll follow up offline.

[12:28] Rachel Kim: And to be clear, incentives are optional and not contingent on what you say.

[12:33] Jules Harding: Of course.

[12:35] Miguel Santos: Alright. Recap: calls-only, 1 per month target, 2 max, no Fridays, Tues/Wed 10–12 PT windows, no recording, avoid incident/billing/roadmap/internal KPIs/compliance, keep it qualitative. Redwood CS moderates. We’ll send updated brief and scripts.

[12:54] Jules Harding: Yep. That all works.

[12:56] Miguel Santos: Perfect. Thanks everyone.
